summary:
House Bill 752, signed by Governor Brad Little and effective 1 July 2026, makes it a crime for a trans person to use a restroom or changing room that does not match their sex assigned at birth. The prohibition reaches government buildings and public-facing private businesses, including gas stations, restaurants, entertainment venues and hospitals. A first offence is a misdemeanour carrying up to one year in jail. Idaho's measure is the only state law extending bathroom criminalisation to private businesses and, according to the ACLU, carries steeper penalties than other states' bans.

Six transgender Idahoans filed suit on 30 April 2026 to block HB 752 before its effect date, arguing the law is unconstitutional and violates due process, equal protection and privacy, and noting it targets no actual criminal conduct. The ACLU of Idaho filed a parallel challenge the same day. National wire reporting covered the legislature's passage of the ban and the jail penalties it carries, along with a lawsuit that has partially blocked it. U.S. District Judge Amanda Brailsford narrowed the law on 16 June 2026, two weeks before it took effect, barring enforcement against single-stall use and against multi-user use where no unoccupied single-user restroom is available on the same floor.

Idaho bans any change of sex on birth certificates. A 2018 implementation law, allowed into legal effect in January 2026, permits only biological male or female sex at birth, reversing a period from 6 April 2018 when trans people could change birth certificates following a 2017 lawsuit. Governor Brad Little's HB 509, signed 30 March 2020, was ruled moot and unenforceable on 7 August 2020 by District Judge David C. Nye, with $321,000 in attorneys' fees awarded to Lambda Legal and approved in August 2022.

Since March 2019 Idaho has offered an "X" third-gender option on driver's licences and state IDs. Under the 7 August 2020 ruling, however, applicants changing a gender marker must submit a physician letter certifying sex reassignment surgery. In November 2019 the Board of Health and Welfare removed the doctor-approval requirement for gender change by transgender minors, retaining parental permission, emancipation or court order.

Gender-affirming medical care for minors is a felony for doctors under HB 71, signed 4 April 2023, which bans puberty blockers, hormones and surgeries; the ban was upheld by the U.S. Supreme Court in April 2024. HB 668, effective 1 July 2024, further restricts care for minors and adults when provided by state, local or county professionals, through Idaho Medicaid, or on state property including hospitals, public colleges and prisons, excluding counselling and mental health but limiting hormone therapy and gender-affirming surgery and barring tax deductibility. An earlier bill, HB 675, which passed the House in March 2022 proposing felony liability and life imprisonment for parents taking children out of state, was blocked by the Senate.

Transgender prisoners were permitted hormone therapy under a September 2024 federal judge ruling that nullified a 1997 law banning it. In August 2024 the Governor signed an executive order barring application within Idaho of any federal laws, regulations and guidelines regarding gender identity or gender ideology.

Under a March 2026 law, schools, childcare providers and medical professionals must out transgender minors to their parents within three days of learning the minor's trans status. An April 2024 law bars teachers and education agencies from using pronouns not based on birth certificates for students. Transgender athletes are barred from public school and university sports teams matching their gender identity under legislation signed 30 March 2020.

No Idaho state law explicitly prohibits discrimination based on gender identity. Federal Title VII protection under Bostock v. Clayton County (15 June 2020) covers workplace discrimination, and roughly 40% of the population is covered by county and city ordinances in Ada County, Bellevue, Boise, Coeur d'Alene, Driggs, Hailey, Idaho Falls, Ketchum, Lewiston, Meridian, Moscow, Pocatello, Sandpoint, Victor, plus Latah County employee protection. Idaho's hate-crime law excludes gender identity, but the federal Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act of October 2009 allows federal prosecution of gender-identity-motivated crimes.
tangentialFactors:
Idaho's HB 752 is the most far-reaching of the state bathroom restrictions now in force nationally, because it reaches private businesses as well as government buildings and attaches jail time to a first offence. The partial injunction issued by Judge Brailsford on 16 June 2026 narrows but does not void the statute, so the operative scope on any given day should be checked before travel.

The state's document regime runs in two directions at once: an X marker remains available on driver's licences and state IDs, while birth certificates are locked to sex assigned at birth and licence gender-marker changes require a physician letter certifying sex reassignment surgery. A visitor relying on an out-of-state licence with an X marker is not governed by Idaho's marker rules, but presentation of documents that do not align with appearance may invite scrutiny in settings where HB 752 applies.

Idaho's August 2024 executive order directing that federal gender-identity law and guidance not be applied within the state sits alongside federal measures that are themselves being litigated, so the interaction between the two layers is unsettled in practice.
localsOnly:
Idaho residents face a birth-certificate regime that permits no change of sex, a felony exposure for doctors providing gender-affirming care to minors, and additional restrictions on care delivered by state or local professionals, through Idaho Medicaid, or on state property. HB 668 also bars tax deductibility for that care.

A March 2026 statute requires schools, childcare providers and medical professionals to disclose a transgender minor's status to parents within three days of learning it. Transgender minors therefore cannot rely on professional confidentiality in educational or clinical settings.

Workplace and housing protection rests on federal Title VII under Bostock and on local ordinances covering about 40% of the population; Idaho has no statewide gender-identity nondiscrimination statute, and its hate-crime law excludes gender identity. Enforcement of gender-identity-motivated crimes can proceed federally under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Act.

Transgender prisoners won hormone-therapy access through a September 2024 federal ruling nullifying a 1997 ban, but the Governor's August 2024 executive order rejecting application of federal gender-identity guidance within Idaho creates conflicting authority on how that right is administered.
outOfScopeNotes:
The scope of HB 752 after Judge Brailsford's 16 June 2026 narrowing is described here from the injunction as reported; the current operative text and any further appellate rulings before or after the 1 July 2026 effect date are not resolved in the sources available.

The ACLU of Idaho suit filed 30 April 2026 and the six-plaintiff suit of the same date are reported as filed; their outcomes are not sourced.

Whether the state's X marker on driver's licences remains available after the January 2026 birth-certificate change, and whether the physician-letter requirement for licence marker changes has been amended since the 2020 ruling, are not resolved in the inventory.

Enforcement data on HB 752, on the three-day outing statute, and on the 2020 sports ban is not present in the sources; no incident counts are available for Idaho specifically.

The interaction between the Governor's August 2024 executive order rejecting federal gender-identity guidance and federal Title VII protection under Bostock is not adjudicated in the sources.
